questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect pertaining to T cell and APC interaction?

options.label: A
options.text: CD80/86 on APCs binding to CD28 on T cells: Essential for activation

options.label: B
options.text: CD40 on APCs binding to CD40L on T cells: Enhances APC function

options.label: C
options.text: PD-L1/PD-L2 on APCs binding to PD-1 on T cells: Induces T cell exhaustion

options.label: D
options.text: CD80/86 on APCs binding to CTLA4 on T cells: Essential for activation

questions.answerText: CD80/86 on APCs binding to CTLA4 on T cells: Essential for activation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans D) CD80/86 on APCs binding to CTLA4 on T cells: Essential for activation

 

CD80/86 on APCs binding to CTLA4 on T cells: Competes with CD28 to INHIBIT activation

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient is scheduled for coagulation studies to assess their clotting function. To prevent blood clotting during the tests, which of the following anticoagulants is commonly used in coagulation studies?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Trisodium citrate

 

This anticoagulant, at a standard concentration of 3.2%, chelates calcium ions, preventing blood clotting during tests such as prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT).

questions.stem: Which of the following is correctly matched with the condition and the genes? APC: Adenomatous polypSTK11: Peutz-Jeghers polypBRAF: Hyperplastic polypSMAD4: Juvenile polyp)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) All 1, 2, 3 and 4

 

1. APC – Adenomatous polyp: Correct.

 

  • APC gene mutation is central to the development of adenomatous polyps, especially in Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP).
  • These polyps follow the adenoma–carcinoma sequence and are premalignant.

 

2. STK11 – Peutz-Jeghers polyp: Correct.

 

  • STK11 (also called LKB1) is the gene mutated in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which features hamartomatous polyps.
  • The polyps typically appear in the small intestine, colon, and stomach, along with mucocutaneous pigmentation.

 

3. BRAF – Hyperplastic polyp (with nuance): Correct — but here's the key clarification:

 

  • While classic hyperplastic polyps are considered non-neoplastic,
  • BRAF mutations can be seen in some types of hyperplastic polyps, particularly those on the serrated pathway.
  • These include sessile serrated adenomas/polyps (SSA/Ps), which may resemble hyperplastic polyps histologically.

 

So, while not all hyperplastic polyps have BRAF mutations, the match is considered valid, especially in proximal colon serrated lesions.

 

4. SMAD4 – Juvenile polyp: Correct.

 

  • SMAD4 (along with BMPR1A) mutations are found in Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome (JPS).
  • The polyps are hamartomatous, and the syndrome increases risk for GI cancers.

 

Final Table:

questions.stem: You are a blood bank officer in the district hospital. ABO incompatibility not seen with
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Cryoprecipitate

 

Cryoprecipitate: Cryoprecipitate is derived from plasma and contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, and other clotting factors. ABO compatibility is generally not considered crucial for cryoprecipitate, as it is often used for specific clotting factor deficiencies and fibrinogen replacement rather than ABO-dependent factors.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP): Plasma component in FFP contains ABO antibodies, and transfusing incompatible plasma can lead to hemolysis.

 

Option B. Platelet Rich Plasma (PRP): Transfusion of ABO-incompatible platelets may result in platelet destruction and reduced effectiveness.

 

Option C. Single Donor Platelets: Similar to PRP, single donor platelets require ABO compatibility to prevent adv reactions. ABO-incompatible platelets can cause immune-mediated platelet destruction.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following trinucleotide repeats with the associated condition:
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C) A – 3, B – 1, C – 2, D - 4

questions.stem: The fluorescent in situ hybridization cannot be useful for detection of which of the following genetic defects?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Point mutation

 

  • FISH is useful for chromosomal anomaly detection like deletion, amplification and translocation. 
  • Single base primer excision test (SBPET), a subtype of PCR based test is done for detection of point mutation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with fatigue, pallor, and jaundice. Laboratory studies reveal anemia, elevated indirect bilirubin, and a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) for IgG. Peripheral blood smear shows spherocytes. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of hemolysis in this patient?

options.label: C
options.text: Oxidative stress leading to Heinz body formation

options.label: D
options.text: Mechanical destruction of red blood cells

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Antibody-mediated extravascular hemolysis

 

Warm AIHA, often associated with SLE, is caused by IgG autoantibodies that bind to red blood cells, leading to extravascular hemolysis (phagocytosis by macrophages in the spleen). Spherocytes and a positive DAT for IgG are characteristic.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis is seen in cold AIHA or PNH, not warm AIHA.

 

Option C. Oxidative stress is seen in G6PD deficiency, leading to Heinz bodies and bite cells, not spherocytes.

 

Option D. Mechanical destruction is seen in MAHA (e.g., TTP, DIC), causing schistocytes, not spherocytes.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of hemoglobinuria, fatigue, and abdominal pain. Laboratory studies reveal pancytopenia, elevated LDH, and a positive sucrose hemolysis test. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the increased risk of thrombosis in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins leading to complement-mediated platelet activation

options.label: C
options.text: Mutation in the JAK2 gene causing hypercoagulability

questions.answerText: Deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins leading to complement-mediated platelet activation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins leading to complement-mediated platelet activation

 

In PNH, the deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins (e.g., CD55, CD59) on platelets and red blood cells leads to uncontrolled complement activation, resulting in hemolysis and platelet activation, which increases the risk of thrombosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Autoantibodies are seen in immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), not PNH.

 

Option C. JAK2 mutation is associated with myeloproliferative disorders, not PNH.

 

Option D. Antithrombin III deficiency is a hereditary thrombophilia unrelated to PNH.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, night sweats, and pruritus. A lymph node biopsy reveals Reed-Sternberg cells positive for CD15 and CD30, with a background of lymphocytes, eosinophils, and plasma cells. Which of the following is the most likely subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma

 

Mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma is characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells in a background of mixed inflammatory cells (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells). It is often associated with B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss).

 

Option A. Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma is characterized by fibrous bands and lacunar-type Reed-Sternberg cells, often involving the mediastinum.

 

Option C. Lymphocyte-rich Hodgkin lymphoma has predominance of lymphocytes & few Reed-Sternberg cells.

 

Option D. Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin lymphoma has few lymphocytes and numerous Reed-Sternberg cells, often seen in advanced disease.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents for routine lab work. The phlebotomist accidentally collects blood for glucose testing in a lavender (EDTA) tube instead of a gray tube. When the glucose result returns, it is falsely low compared to the patient's previous values. Which of the following best explains the reason for this discrepancy?

options.label: A
options.text: EDTA chelates calcium, preventing glycolysis in red blood cells

options.label: B
options.text: EDTA inhibits glucose oxidation, leading to artificially low readings

options.label: C
options.text: Glycolysis continues in RBCs in the absence of an inhibitor, consuming glucose

options.label: D
options.text: EDTA causes RBC lysis, releasing intracellular contents that dilute glucose levels

questions.answerText: Glycolysis continues in RBCs in the absence of an inhibitor, consuming glucose
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Glycolysis continues in RBCs in the absence of an inhibitor, consuming glucose

 

Glycolysis continues in RBCs in the absence of an inhibitor, consuming glucose – Correct. The gray-top tube contains sodium fluoride, which inhibits glycolysis by blocking enolase. Without this inhibitor, RBCs continue metabolizing glucose, leading to falsely low results.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. EDTA chelates calcium, preventing glycolysis in red blood cells:  Incorrect. EDTA does chelate calcium, but this affects coagulation rather than glucose preservation.

 

Option B. EDTA inhibits glucose oxidation, leading to artificially low reading:  Incorrect. EDTA does not inhibit glucose metabolism; instead, it prevents clotting.

 

Option D. EDTA causes RBC lysis, releasing intracellular contents that dilute glucose levels: Incorrect. While EDTA can cause hemolysis, this would not lead to a decrease in glucose but could interfere with potassium or LDH measurements.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with a palpable lump in her left breast with bloody nipple discharge. A core needle biopsy is performed, and histopathology reveals sheets of small, pleomorphic cells infiltrating the stroma with the formation of glandular structures. Which of the following is not true for her?

options.label: A
options.text: Diamino benzidine is used for brown color in IHC.

options.label: B
options.text: For a score 2 in IHC, Fluorescence in situ hybridization is indicated.

options.label: C
options.text: Under activity of CDH1 gene tends to be bilateral and multifocal.

options.label: D
options.text: Over expression of E cadherin has association with familial gastric cancer.

questions.answerText: Over expression of E cadherin has association with familial gastric cancer.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Over expression of E cadherin has association with familial gastric cancer.

 

Under activity of E cadherin has association with familial gastric cancer.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child of Bengali descent presents with mild fatigue and pallor. Laboratory results show a hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL, MCV of 68 fL, and an RBC count of 5.8 million cells/µL. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. B) β-thalassemia minor

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents with bone pain, anemia, and recurrent infections. Laboratory tests reveal a serum creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL and hypercalcemia. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M-spike, and urine protein electrophoresis is positive for Bence-Jones proteins. Which of the following findings would be most indicative of the underlying pathophysiology in this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased production of immunoglobulin G polyclonal antibodies

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Elevated serum levels of β2-microglobulin

 

MM has monoclonal proliferation of plasma cells, which produce a single type of immunoglobulin, leading to the M-spike seen on electrophoresis. β2-microglobulin levels correlate with tumor burden and are often elevated in multiple myeloma, serving as a prognostic marker.

questions.stem: Pick the incorrect statements about hemolytic anemia: Sickle cell anemia has high osmotic fragility and reduced mechanical fragility Increased HbA2 is seen with iron deficiency anemia Mentzer index helps in differentiation of thalassemia trait from iron deficiency anemia Donath Landsteiner antibody is seen in PCH
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) 1 and 2

 

SCA has High MF..low OF…IDA has reduced HbA2..DL antibody is cold hemolysin disease

questions.stem: 60-year-old female with a history of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease presents with abdominal discomfort and elevated blood pressure. Pick the true statements about her condition She may have a mutation in the short arm of chromosome 3High risk of papillary carcinoma of the kidney Histology shows plant like cells with perinuclear haloCells have high glycogen and fat inside them
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Only 1 and 4

 

Clear cell cancer has VHL gene mutation on 3p…

questions.stem: A 24-year-old male presents with osteomas of the mandible, multiple epidermoid cysts, and supernumerary teeth. His father had a history of colorectal cancer at age 40. Colonoscopy reveals numerous adenomatous polyps throughout the colon. Genetic analysis confirms a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 5q21. Which of the following additional conditions is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Desmoid tumors

 

Desmoid tumors: Correct. Patients with Gardner syndrome (a variant of FAP) are at high risk of developing desmoid tumors, which are locally aggressive fibromatoses commonly found in the abdomen.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Medulloblastoma: Incorrect. Although FAP is associated with the Turcot syndrome variant, where medulloblastomas or glioblastomas can occur, this patient's findings (osteomas, epidermoid cysts, supernumerary teeth) are more consistent with Gardner syndrome, which is a subtype of FAP.

 

Option B. Gastric signet-ring cell carcinoma: Incorrect. This is more commonly associated with hereditary diffuse gastric cancer (CDH1 gene mutation) rather than FAP.

 

Option D. Pheochromocytoma: Incorrect. Pheochromocytomas are associated with MEN2 (RET mutation) and VHL syndrome, but not FAP.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, including Aspergillus pneumonia and Staphylococcus abscesses. Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test is negative, and dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry shows reduced fluorescence. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Defective myeloperoxidase enzyme leading to impaired hypochlorous acid production

options.label: B
options.text: Mutation in NADPH oxidase resulting in defective superoxide production

options.label: C
options.text: Impaired migration of neutrophils due to defective β2 integrins (CD18 mutation)

options.label: D
options.text: Lack of B cells due to a mutation in the Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) gene

questions.answerText: Mutation in NADPH oxidase resulting in defective superoxide production
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Mutation in NADPH oxidase resulting in defective superoxide production

 

Mutation in NADPH oxidase – Correct. Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is caused by an X-linked or autosomal recessive mutation in NADPH oxidase, leading to defective respiratory burst and recurrent catalase-positive bacterial/fungal infections. The NBT test is negative, and DHR flow cytometry shows decreased fluorescence.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Defective myeloperoxidase enzyme: Incorrect. Myeloperoxidase deficiency results in mild immunodeficiency but does not cause a negative NBT test.

 

Option C. Impaired neutrophil migration (CD18 defect): Incorrect. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD) presents with delayed umbilical cord separation, leukocytosis, and recurrent bacterial infections, but it does not affect respiratory burst.

 

Option D. Lack of B cells (BTK mutation): Incorrect. X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA) causes sinopulmonary and enteroviral infections, but does not affect neutrophil function or respiratory burst.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteosarcoma and a glioblastoma within the same year. Her father died of a sarcoma at age 40, and her younger sister has been treated for breast cancer at age 32. Which of the following genetic alterations is most likely responsible for this family’s cancer predisposition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) p53 gene mutation

 

p53 mutation: Correct. Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) is caused by a TP53 mutation, predisposing individuals to osteosarcoma, breast cancer, glioblastomas, and adrenocortical carcinomas. p53 is known as the "guardian of the genome" because it induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in response to DNA damage.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. STK11 mutation: Incorrect. This is seen in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which causes GI hamartomas and mucocutaneous pigmentation, not a predisposition to multiple sarcomas and brain tumors.

 

Option C. APC mutation : Incorrect. This is associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) and colorectal cancer but does not predispose to osteosarcomas or brain tumors.

 

Option D. BRCA1 mutation : Incorrect. BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations increase the risk of breast and ovarian cancer, but do not explain this patient's sarcomas and brain tumors.

questions.stem: A new chemotherapy drug is being developed to treat pancreatic adenocarcinoma. It works by increasing the expression of pro-apoptotic proteins. Which of the following proteins is most likely activated by this drug to induce apoptosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) FasL

 

FasL: Correct. Fas ligand (FasL) binds to the Fas (CD95) death receptor, leading to caspase activation and apoptosis via the extrinsic pathway. Many cancers evade apoptosis by downregulating Fas expression.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bcl-2 : Incorrect. Bcl-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein, preventing cytochrome c release and caspase activation. Overexpression of Bcl-2 is seen in follicular lymphoma (t(14;18)), contributing to chemotherapy resistance.

 

Option C. FLIP : Incorrect. FLIP inhibits apoptosis by blocking caspase-8 activation in the extrinsic pathway.

 

Option D. NF-κB : Incorrect. NF-κB promotes cell survival and inflammation, protecting tumor cells from apoptosis.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old male undergoes a nephrectomy for a renal mass. Histopathology reveals large, pale eosinophilic cells with prominent cell membranes and a perinuclear halo. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most commonly associated with this tumor?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Multiple chromosome losses (monosomy of 1, 2, 6, 10, 17, and Y)

 

Multiple chromosome losses : Correct. Chromophobe RCC is characterized by loss of multiple chromosomes, leading to its distinct perinuclear halo and eosinophilic cytoplasm on histology.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. VHL mutation : Incorrect. Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) mutation is associated with clear cell renal carcinoma, not chromophobe RCC.

 

Option B. FH mutation : Incorrect. Fumarate hydratase (FH) mutation is seen in hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (HLRCC), which presents with papillary RCC.

 

Option C. TSC1/TSC2 mutation : Incorrect. Tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutation) is associated with angiomyolipomas, not RCC.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old female non-smoker presents with cough, weight loss, and hemoptysis. Imaging reveals a peripheral lung mass, and biopsy confirms lung adenocarcinoma. Molecular testing is performed for a mutation that makes the tumor susceptible to targeted therapy. Which of the following mutations is not likely to be present in this cancer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) BRAF

 

BRAF V600E mutations are more common in melanoma and some colorectal cancers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. KRAS: Mutations are more common in smokers and are associated with poor prognosis.

 

Option B. EGFR: Non-smokers and make tumors susceptible to EGFR inhibitors (erlotinib, gefitinib).

 

Option D. ALK: Incorrect. ALK rearrangements (EML4-ALK fusion) occur in young non-smokers and are treated with ALK inhibitors (crizotinib).

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a history of easy bruising, frequent nosebleeds, and prolonged bleeding after dental procedures. Laboratory testing reveals: PT: 12 sec (Normal)aPTT: 45 sec (Elevated)Platelet count: NormalBleeding time: ProlongedRistocetin cofactor assay: Decreased Which of the following best explains this patient’s bleeding disorder?

options.label: D
options.text: Deficiency of thrombin activation of Factor V

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Impaired platelet glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) binding

 

Impaired platelet glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) binding : Correct. von Willebrand factor (vWF) binds to GpIb to mediate platelet adhesion. Deficiency or dysfunction of vWF leads to prolonged bleeding time and defective platelet aggregation.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Deficiency of fibrin-stabilizing factor (Factor XIII): Incorrect. Factor XIII deficiency causes delayed wound healing, not mucocutaneous bleeding.

 

Option C. Antibody-mediated platelet destruction: Incorrect. This describes immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), which presents with low platelet count.

 

Option D. Deficiency of thrombin activation of Factor V : Incorrect. Factor V is activated by thrombin in secondary hemostasis, but von Willebrand disease affects primary hemostasis.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with a recent history of untreated streptococcal pharyngitis presents with exertional dyspnea and a new murmur. Echocardiography reveals thickened mitral valve leaflets with small vegetations along the line of closure. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of these vegetations?

options.label: A
options.text: Deposition of sterile platelet-fibrin thrombi due to hypercoagulability

options.label: B
options.text: Direct bacterial invasion leading to large, destructive vegetations

options.label: C
options.text: Immune-mediated inflammatory damage leading to fibrinoid necrosis

options.label: D
options.text: Aggregation of mucopolysaccharides within the valve matrix

questions.answerText: Immune-mediated inflammatory damage leading to fibrinoid necrosis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Immune-mediated inflammatory damage leading to fibrinoid necrosis

 

Immune-mediated inflammatory damage : Correct. Acute rheumatic fever involves molecular mimicry between streptococcal M protein and cardiac myosin, leading to fibrinoid necrosis and small vegetations.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sterile platelet-fibrin thrombi : Incorrect. This describes nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) in hypercoagulable states.

 

Option B. Direct bacterial invasion : Incorrect. Bacterial endocarditis causes large, friable vegetations, not the small ones seen in rheumatic heart disease.

 

Option D. Mucopolysaccharide aggregation : Incorrect. This describes myxomatous degeneration, which occurs in mitral valve prolapse, not rheumatic disease.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with SLE presents with recurrent miscarriages and deep vein thrombosis. Laboratory findings include: ANA: PositiveAnti-dsDNA: PositiveAnticardiolipin antibody: PositiveProlonged aPTT Which of the following mechanisms best explains her clinical manifestations?

options.label: A
options.text: Complement-mediated immune complex deposition in endothelium

options.label: C
options.text: Antibody-mediated activation of tissue factor and endothelial damage

options.label: D
options.text: Direct T-cell cytotoxicity against endothelial cells

questions.answerText: Antibody-mediated activation of tissue factor and endothelial damage
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Antibody-mediated activation of tissue factor and endothelial damage

 

Antibody-mediated activation of tissue factor : Correct. Antiphospholipid antibodies (e.g., anticardiolipin, lupus anticoagulant) cause endothelial damage, increasing thrombosis risk.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Complement-mediated immune complex deposition: Incorrect. This occurs in glomerulonephritis and cutaneous lupus, not thrombosis.

 

Option B. Impaired opsonization of apoptotic debris: Incorrect. This is involved in SLE pathogenesis but does not explain the hypercoagulability.

 

Option D. Direct T-cell cytotoxicity: Incorrect. Cytotoxic T cells are involved in Type IV hypersensitivity, not in SLE autoantibody-mediated thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral ulcers, photosensitivity, and polyarthritis. Genetic analysis reveals a Fas (CD95) receptor mutation leading to defective apoptotic signaling in autoreactive T cells. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of loss of immune tolerance in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Failure of peripheral deletion of autoreactive lymphocytes

options.label: B
options.text: Increased activity of regulatory T cells

options.label: C
options.text: Defective thymic selection leading to autoreactive lymphocyte escape

options.label: D
options.text: Enhanced somatic hypermutation in germinal centers

questions.answerText: Failure of peripheral deletion of autoreactive lymphocytes
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Failure of peripheral deletion of autoreactive lymphocytes

 

Failure of peripheral deletion : Correct. Fas mutations impair peripheral tolerance, preventing apoptosis of autoreactive T cells, leading to autoimmune diseases like SLE.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Increased regulatory T cell activity : Incorrect. Regulatory T cells suppress autoimmunity, not promote it.

 

Option C. Defective thymic selection : Incorrect. AIRE mutations (not Fas mutations) cause central tolerance failure, leading to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APS-1).

 

Option D. Enhanced somatic hypermutation : Incorrect. Somatic hypermutation increases antibody diversity but does not directly cause tolerance loss.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man presents for an annual check-up. He is asymptomatic, but biopsy of his myocardium reveals yellow-brown perinuclear granules within cardiomyocytes. Which of the following best explains the formation of these granules?

options.label: A
options.text: Iron accumulation due to defective lysosomal degradation

options.label: B
options.text: Autoimmune-mediated damage leading to intracellular debris accumulation

options.label: C
options.text: Lipid peroxidation and oxidative damage of cellular organelles

options.label: D
options.text: Mutations in lysosomal enzymes leading to incomplete degradation of sphingolipids

questions.answerText: Lipid peroxidation and oxidative damage of cellular organelles
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Lipid peroxidation and oxidative damage of cellular organelles

 

Lipid peroxidation : Correct. Lipofuscin is an “aging pigment” formed due to oxidative damage of phospholipids, leading to indigestible residues accumulating in lysosomes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Iron accumulation : Incorrect. This describes hemosiderin deposition seen in hemochromatosis, not lipofuscin.

 

Option B. Autoimmune-mediated damage : Incorrect. Autoimmune diseases do not cause lipofuscin accumulation.

 

Option D. Lysosomal enzyme mutation : Incorrect. Lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Gaucher, Tay-Sachs) cause accumulation of specific metabolic products, not lipofuscin.

questions.stem: Epithelial mesenchymal transcription is mediated by which transcription factors?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. B) SNAIL & TWIST

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presented to you with weakness, neuropathy in his bilateral lower limbs and a positive Romberg sign. He has a history of gastrectomy for stomach polyp. He is likely deficient in which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C) Vitamin B12 deficiency

questions.stemHtml: Match the following hemoglobin variants with their corresponding amino acid substitution:
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. D) A – 2, B – 1, C – 3, D - 4

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with generalized erythroderma, intense pruritus, and diffuse lymphadenopathy. Peripheral smear shows circulating cerebriform nuclei (Sezary cells). Which of the following markers is most likely positive?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) CD4

 

Sezary syndrome is a leukemic variant of Mycosis Fungoides, a CD4+ T-cell lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man presents with B symptoms and hepatosplenomegaly. Lymph node biopsy reveals large pleomorphic cells with horseshoe-shaped nuclei (hallmark cells). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Anaplastic large cell lymphoma

 

ALK-positive anaplastic large cell lymphoma is a CD30+ T-cell lymphoma with hallmark cells and ALK gene rearrangement.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presents with headache, blurred vision, and mucosal bleeding. Serum electrophoresis reveals an IgM monoclonal spike. What is the underlying condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Waldenström macroglobulinemia

 

Hyperviscosity symptoms with IgM monoclonal gammopathy is Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with splenomegaly, anemia, and lymphocytosis. Flow cytometry shows CD5+, CD19+, CD20+, CD23- B cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Mantle cell lymphoma

 

Mantle cell lymphoma is a CD5+ but CD23- B-cell lymphoma, distinguished from CLL (which is CD23+).

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy from Uganda presents with a rapidly enlarging jaw mass. Biopsy of the lesion shows sheets of medium-sized lymphoid cells with high mitotic activity and interspersed tingible body macrophages. Which chromosomal translocation is most likely present?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) t(8;14)

 

Burkitt lymphoma is associated with t(8;14), leading to MYC oncogene overexpression. The endemic form (African) often presents as a jaw or facial tumor and is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection…, creating a "starry sky" appearance

questions.stem: A 50 year-old man with CKD receives a blood transfusion. Thirty minutes into the transfusion, he develops chills, a fever of 101°F, and mild hypotension. The transfusion is stopped, and there are no signs of hemolysis. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of his reaction?

options.label: A
options.text: Alloantibodies directed against donor red blood cell antigens

options.label: B
options.text: Release of cytokines from donor leukocytes during storage

options.label: C
options.text: IgG antibodies that recognize IgA in the infused blood product

options.label: D
options.text: Activation of HLA antibodies on the neutrophils of recipient

questions.answerText: Release of cytokines from donor leukocytes during storage
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Release of cytokines from donor leukocytes during storage

 

FNHTR is due to release of cytokines from donor leukocytes during storage (Leukoreduction before storage can reduce this risk.)

 

Other Options:

 

Option d…TRALI…..option C ..anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of hematologic malignancy receives a transfusion of 2 units of blood. Three weeks later, he develops a high fever, rash, jaundice, and pancytopenia. Bone marrow biopsy shows hypocellularity. Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measure to reduce the risk of this transfusion complication?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Irradiation of blood products

 

GVHD can be reduced by irradiation.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a painless neck mass. Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the nodule reveals papillary thyroid carcinoma with nuclear grooves and intranuclear inclusions. A total thyroidectomy is performed, and pathology confirms a 2.5 cm tumor without extrathyroidal extension. Further genetic analysis reveals a BRAF V600E mutation in the tumor cells. Which of the following is true about this cancer?

options.label: B
options.text: Better response to radioactive iodine therapy

options.label: D
options.text: Increased risk of aggressive histologic variants

questions.answerText: Increased risk of aggressive histologic variants
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Increased risk of aggressive histologic variants

 

The BRAF V600E mutation in papillary thyroid carcinoma is associated with more aggressive disease, including an increased risk of certain histologic variants, such as the tall cell variant, which are more likely to exhibit aggressive behavior. Patients with BRAF-mutated tumors often have higher recurrence rates and may show poorer responses to radioactive iodine therapy.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following symptoms is least likely to be observed in a patient diagnosed with the flow cytometry pattern as shown in the image.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not correctly matched?

options.label: A
options.text: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation: skin rash after wasp bite

options.label: B
options.text: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity: penicillin induced hemolytic anemia

options.label: C
options.text: Immune complex deposition: thrombocytopenia in SLE patients

options.label: D
options.text: T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity: Contact dermatitis due to poison ivy

questions.answerText: Immune complex deposition: thrombocytopenia in SLE patients
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Immune complex deposition: thrombocytopenia in SLE patients

 

  • Immune complex deposition (Type III hypersensitivity) in SLE causes:
  • Glomerulonephritis, arthritis, vasculitis, serositis
  • But thrombocytopenia in SLE is usually due to:
  • Type II hypersensitivity: autoantibodies against platelet antigens → destruction by splenic macrophages

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation: skin rash after wasp bite: Correctly matched 

 

  • This is a classic Type I hypersensitivity reaction, where:
  • IgE binds to mast cells
  • Allergen (wasp venom) triggers immediate degranulation
  • Symptoms: rash, urticaria, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis

 

Option B. Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC): penicillin-induced hemolytic anemia: Correctly matched 

 

  • Penicillin binds to RBCs, forming a hapten complex → IgG binds → attracts NK cells/macrophages via Fc receptors → cell lysis
  • This is a Type II hypersensitivity reaction involving ADCC

 

Option D. T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity: Contact dermatitis due to poison ivy: Correctly matched 

 

  • This is a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction:
  • T-cell mediated (CD8+ and Th1)
  • Delayed onset (48–72 hours)
  • Caused by haptens like urushiol in poison ivy binding skin proteins

questions.stem: A 3-month-old boy presents with recurrent viral, bacterial, and fungal infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. Laboratory tests show low T-cell and B-cell counts, absent thymic shadow on chest X-ray and hypogammaglobulinemia. Flow cytometry confirms a marked decrease in CD3+ T cells. Which of the following is the most likely underlying genetic defect?

options.label: A
options.text: Mutation in the common gamma chain (IL-2Rγ)

options.label: C
options.text: Loss-of-function mutation in BTK (Bruton’s tyrosine kinase)

questions.answerText: Mutation in the common gamma chain (IL-2Rγ)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Mutation in the common gamma chain (IL-2Rγ)

 

IL-2Rγ mutation: Correct. The most common cause of SCID is an X-linked mutation in the IL-2 receptor gamma chain, which affects multiple cytokine signaling pathways and leads to profound T-cell and B-cell dysfunction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. ADA deficiency: Incorrect. Also causes SCID, is less common, AR, and is associated with toxic purine metabolite accumulation.

 

Option C. BTK mutation: Incorrect. BTK mutation causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA), which affects B cells but not T cells.

 

Option D. WASP mutation: Incorrect. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome leads to thrombocytopenia, eczema, and immunodeficiency, but not the combined B and T cell defect seen in SCID.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old male collapses while playing basketball. He is resuscitated and found to have a harsh systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva. Echocardiography reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. A myocardial biopsy is performed. Which of the following histological findings is most characteristic of this patient’s disease?

options.label: B
options.text: Myofibrillar loss and vacuolization of cardiomyocytes

options.label: C
options.text: Patchy inflammatory infiltrates with multinucleated giant cells

options.label: D
options.text: Endocardial fibroelastosis with thickening of the ventricular walls

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Myocyte disarray with interstitial fibrosis

 

Myocyte disarray with interstitial fibrosis – Correct. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is characterized by myocyte disarray, hypertrophic myocytes arranged in chaotic, disorganized patterns, and interstitial fibrosis.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Myofibrillar loss and vacuolization: Incorrect. Seen in DCM due to mitochondrial dysfunction or toxic cardiomyopathies (e.g., anthracyclines).

 

Option C. Patchy inflammatory infiltrates with giant cells: Incorrect. Giant cell myocarditis is an aggressive, immune-mediated myocarditis, not HCM.

 

Option D. Endocardial fibroelastosis: Incorrect. Seen in RCM particularly in infants, and is unrelated to HCM.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue. Laboratory tests show iron deficiency anemia. Serologic testing is positive for anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Duodenal biopsy is performed. Which of the following histological findings is most characteristic of this patient’s disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis

options.label: B
options.text: Foamy macrophages in the lamina propria containing PAS-positive granules

options.label: C
options.text: Marked eosinophilic infiltration of the lamina propria

options.label: D
options.text: Blunted villi with coccobacilli seen on electron microscopy

questions.answerText: Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis

 

Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytosis – Correct. Celiac disease is characterized by loss of villi, compensatory crypt elongation, and increased intraepithelial CD8+ lymphocytes.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Foamy macrophages with PAS-positive granules: Incorrect. Seen in Whipple disease.

 

Option C. Marked eosinophilic infiltration: Incorrect. Seen in eosinophilic gastroenteritis, not celiac sprue.

 

Option D. Blunted villi with coccobacilli: Incorrect. Seen in tropical sprue.

Colonoscopy reveals an ulcer in the terminal ileum with a heaped-up margin and surrounding inflammation. Biopsy of the ulcer base shows caseating granulomas and acid-fast bacilli. Which of the following best describes the characteristic histological feature of this condition?

Option A. Transmural inflammation with creeping fat: Incorrect. Characteristic of Crohn disease.

 

Option B. Flask-shaped ulcers with trophozoites: Incorrect. Seen in amoebiasis.

 

Option C. Linear ulcers along the mesenteric border: Incorrect. Associated with typhoid fever.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is associated with a bone marrow aspirate having the finding as shown in the image.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Chronic myeloid leukemia

 

Gaucher cells exhibit diffuse iron staining whereas pseudo-Gaucher cells do not. Electron microscopy shows that Gaucher cells contain typical tubular cytoplasmic inclusions absent in pseudo-Gaucher cells. These cannot be differentiated by routine H&E staining

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the dermatologist for evaluation of severe sunburns after minimal sun exposure. He has freckling, dry skin, and multiple areas of hyperpigmentation on his face and arms. His family history is significant for a sibling who developed skin cancer at an early age. Genetic testing reveals a mutation affecting nucleotide excision repair. Which of the following molecular defects is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Defective mismatch repair of microsatellite sequences

options.label: B
options.text: Deficient homologous recombination for double-strand DNA breaks

options.label: C
options.text: Impaired removal of pyrimidine dimers caused by ultraviolet radiation

options.label: D
options.text: Failure to repair DNA interstrand crosslinks involving fanconi anemia genes

questions.answerText: Impaired removal of pyrimidine dimers caused by ultraviolet radiation
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Impaired removal of pyrimidine dimers caused by ultraviolet radiation

 

Impaired removal of pyrimidine dimers caused by ultraviolet radiation – Correct. This describes XP caused by defective nucleotide excision repair, leading to extreme UV sensitivity and skin cancer risk.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Defective mismatch repair of microsatellite sequences: Incorrect. Seen in Lynch syndrome (HNPCC), which predisposes to colorectal and endometrial cancer.

 

Option B. Deficient homologous recombination for double-strand DNA breaks: Incorrect. Seen in Fanconi anemia and BRCA mutations.

 

Option D. Failure to repair DNA interstrand crosslinks involving Fanconi anemia genes: Incorrect. Seen in Fanconi anemia, characterized by bone marrow failure and congenital abnormalities.

questions.stemHtml: A patient suffered from severe chest pain, diaphoresis, nausea and expired. Which of the following is the likely age of infarct from the image of the cardiac biopsy shown here?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2-3 days

 

Brisk infiltration is see with 2-3 days but if not given as an option, 1 day would be the answer.

questions.stem: A 30 year old patient with pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis, palpable purpura, myalgia and pulmonary hemorrhage and was found to have p-ANCA positivity. Which of the following is the likely vasculitis in him?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Microscopic polyangiitis

 

Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is a small-vessel vasculitis characterized by the presence of p-ANCA with MPO specificity. It often presents with systemic symptoms like joint pain and skin purpura as well as RPGN (consistent with the diffuse glomerular inflammation and necrotizing glomerulonephritis observed in the biopsy).

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with fever for 6 days, conjunctival injection, rash, erythematous lips and tongue, and swelling of the hands and feet. Cervical lymphadenopathy is present. His fever does not respond to antibiotics. Laboratory findings include thrombocytosis and elevated ESR. Which of the following is the most significant complication of this disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Coronary artery aneurysm

 

Coronary artery aneurysm: Correct. Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis affecting the coronary arteries, leading to aneurysms and risk of myocardial infarction.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Aortic dissection: Incorrect. Seen in Marfan syndrome, not Kawasaki disease.

 

Option C. Pulmonary embolism: Incorrect. Not a primary complication of Kawasaki disease.

 

Option D. Glomerulonephritis: Incorrect. Seen in immune complex diseases like SLEbut not Kawasaki disease.

questions.solutionHtml:

questions.stemHtml: A patient underwent cystoscopy, which showed multiple yellow-white plaques in the trigone of the bladder. The histopathology image is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Malakoplakia 

 

  • Malakoplakia is a rare condition of unknown etiology (observed in immunocompromised patients and transplant recipients) primarily affecting the urinary bladder. It is likely associated with chronic inflammation and defective phagocytosis by macrophages.
  • On cystoscopy, malakoplakia appears as multiple yellow-white plaques in the bladder trigone.The lesions are soft, flat, and slightly raised, with sizes ranging from 0.5 to 5 cm.
  • Histopathologically, malakoplakia shows massive accumulation of foamy macrophages, multinucleate giant cells, and lymphocytes. MG bodies (cytoplasmic laminated concretions of calcium phosphate, are seen within macrophages and represent lysosomes filled with partially digested debris of bacteria, resulting from defective phagocytosis.

questions.stem: A female patient presented with fatigue. Routine complete blood count analysis showed hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, MCV 60fL, and RBC count of 5.2 million. A peripheral smear showed microcytic hypochromic anemia. Which of the following is the next best investigation for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) HbA2 levels 

 

A peripheral blood smear with microcytic hypochromic cells and a Mentzer index of less than 13 indicates thalassemia. As a result, HbA2 levels (which are elevated in thalassemia) must be tested next

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with painless waxing and waning lymphadenopathy for the past 6 months. A lymph node biopsy shows nodular architecture with small cleaved cells and large non-cleaved cells. Immunophenotyping is CD10+, CD19+, CD20+ with a t(14;18) translocation. Which of the following best distinguishes this condition from reactive follicular hyperplasia?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) BCL-2 positivity in follicular centers

 

Follicular lymphoma is driven by t(14;18), leading to overexpression of BCL-2, which inhibits apoptosis. Unlike reactive follicular hyperplasia (which has BCL-2-negative follicles), follicular lymphoma has BCL-2 positivity within germinal centers.
